passage:
Note from Amandeep, class teacher:
At home time, Chandrika was near the gate when a man she did not know said, "Come, I have sweets. Your mother sent me." She looked at the sweets, then at me, frowning, and pulled at her bag strap. Then she said "No," ran to me and told me what he had said. I kept her beside me, told her she had done nothing wrong, and alerted the gate guard, the head teacher and her mother. Next day I taught the class: refuse, go straight to a grown-up you trust, and tell them. Any grown-up wanting a child's secret or favour is a warning sign.

qa.q: What did the man say to Chandrika at the gate?
qa.a: He said, "Come, I have sweets. Your mother sent me."

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she looked at the sweets and then at Amandeep?
qa.a: She seemed tempted and confused, since she frowned and pulled at her bag strap before deciding.

qa.q: What rule did Amandeep teach the class the next day?
qa.a: Refuse, go straight to a grown-up you trust, and tell them, because any grown-up wanting a child's secret or favour is a warning sign. 🤍

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother see what Chandrika did?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved and proud that Chandrika said no and told the teacher, as she was told straight away.

grounding: A stranger offers sweets and claims the mother sent him; the child feels confused, says no, runs to a trusted adult and tells.

passage:
"Ramesh? Ramesh! Your mother sent me. Come, I have sweets in the car."
Ramesh stood by the school gate, holding his bag. The man held out a packet of toffees. Ramesh looked at the toffees. His tummy felt funny.
"Mummy always comes herself."
"She's busy. Come quickly."
"No!" Ramesh ran back inside the gate to Anirban Sir.
"Sir! A man says Mummy sent him. He has sweets."
Anirban Sir held Ramesh's hand and stepped to the gate. The car drove off fast.
"You did exactly right," Anirban Sir said. He called Ramesh's mother at once and told the principal, who phoned the police.

qa.q: What did the man hold out to Ramesh?
qa.a: He held out a packet of toffees.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he looked at the toffees?
qa.a: He felt tempted and confused, with a funny feeling in his tummy that something wasn't right.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do, and why was it right?
qa.a: He said no, ran to Anirban Sir and told him; a stranger who says a parent sent them and offers sweets is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Anirban Sir feel watching the car drive off?
qa.a: He is likely alarmed but relieved Ramesh came to him, which is why he acts at once to call Ramesh's mother and the principal.

grounding: A stranger offers a young boy sweets and says his mother sent him; he says no, runs to a teacher and tells, and the adults act immediately.

passage:
Note from Shankar Sir, class teacher, to Charu's parents.
At afternoon play today, a woman leaned over the park railing and called to Charu, "Can you help me find my puppy? Come quickly, don't tell anyone." Charu looked confused and took a step, then stopped. She ran to me and said, "A lady wants me to help find a puppy. She said don't tell." I brought all the children in, told the principal and security at once, and the woman left. I told Charu, "Grown-ups should ask grown-ups for help, never children. You did the right thing." Please tell her again tonight how proud you are.

qa.q: What did the woman ask Charu to help find?
qa.a: She asked Charu to help find her puppy.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when the woman called her?
qa.a: She felt confused and a little tempted, taking a step before she stopped.

qa.q: What rule did Shankar Sir give Charu?
qa.a: Grown-ups should ask grown-ups for help, never children, and asking for secrecy is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel frightened by what nearly happened but proud and relieved that Charu stopped and told her teacher.

grounding: A stranger asks a young girl for help and secrecy; she runs to her teacher and tells, and the teacher acts at once.
